record.answer_text:
Found 1 pubmed record: Significantly increased load of hereditary cancer-linked germline variants in infertile men. [2]. 

Study findings

The study compared germline pathogenic and likely pathogenic variant burden across hereditary cancer genes between infertile and fertile men, finding a substantially higher rate of disease-causing findings in infertile men than fertile men [1]. The analysis covered a defined panel of hereditary cancer genes examined in a cohort of infertile and fertile men [1]. The elevated variant load in infertile men spanned a substantial number of distinct cancer-related genes [1]. No difference in finding prevalence was observed between azoospermic and oligozoospermic men, and no enrichment was seen among men with a history of cryptorchidism [1].

llm.reply:
I could not find information on this.

The findings returned for this query concern hereditary cancer gene variants in infertile men [1][2][3] and do not address Lynch syndrome's causal genes, its condition record, clinical variants, or current trials.

The retrieved literature for this question does not directly address Lynch syndrome's causal genes, its condition record, clinical variants, or current trials; instead, the search returned a single publication on hereditary cancer gene variants in infertile men [1].

## Study identified

The paper retrieved is titled Significantly increased load of hereditary cancer-linked germline variants in infertile men [1]. It corresponds to Publication pmid: 40060932 [3].

## Study findings

The study compared germline pathogenic and likely pathogenic variant burden across hereditary cancer genes between infertile and fertile men, finding a substantially higher rate of disease-causing findings in infertile men than fertile men [2: "This study showed almost 5-fold enrichment of disease-causing findings in hereditary cancer genes in infertile compared to fertile men (6.9% vs 1.5%, P = 2.3 × 10-4)"]. The analysis covered a defined panel of hereditary cancer genes examined in a cohort of infertile and fertile men [2: "This retrospective study analyzed germline likely pathogenic and pathogenic (LP/P) variants in 157 hereditary cancer genes in 522 infertile and 323 fertile men recruited to the ESTonian ANDrology (ESTAND) cohort"]. The elevated variant load in infertile men spanned a substantial number of distinct cancer-related genes [2: "Infertile men presented a nearly 5-fold higher load of LP/P findings (36 of 522 cases, 6.9%) compared to fertile subjects (5 of 323, 1.5%; odds ratio (OR) = 4.7, 95% CI 1.81-15.5; P = 2.3 × 10-4) spanning over 24 hereditary cancer genes"]. No difference in finding prevalence was observed between azoospermic and oligozoospermic men, and no enrichment was seen among men with a history of cryptorchidism [2: "The prevalence of findings was not significantly different between azoospermic and oligozoospermic cases. There was also no enrichment of findings in men with a history of cryptorchidism"].

## Relevance to Lynch syndrome

This paper does not name Lynch syndrome, its causal genes, a condition record, clinical variants specific to it, or any related clinical trials, so no findings on those specific points were retrieved [1][2][3].
